record.paper_title: The Hidden Subgroup Problem - Review and Open Problems
record.original_question: For black-box group algorithms whose current proofs use only the abelian quantum Fourier transform, does replacing that step with genuinely nonabelian quantum Fourier transforms lead to stronger algorithmic results or more efficient hidden-subgroup procedures?

evidence.quote: A question remains: the above proofs only use the abelian QFT to get the results. Does using the nonabelian QFTs give better results?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let G be a finite group given as a black box: group elements are encoded as bit strings, and oracles perform multiplication, inversion, and equality testing. A subgroup H ≤ G is "hidden" by a function f : G → S (S a finite set) if f is constant on each left coset of H and distinct on different cosets; the hidden subgroup problem (HSP) asks to determine H (e.g., a generating set) using queries to f and group operations.

Quantum Fourier transforms. For a finite abelian group A, the abelian quantum Fourier transform QFT_A is the unitary on C[A] sending |a⟩ to |A|^{-1/2} Σ_{χ ∈ Â} χ(a) |χ⟩, where Â is the character group. For a general (possibly nonabelian) finite group G, a nonabelian QFT_G is a unitary on C[G] that, with respect to a chosen system of irreducible unitary representations {ρ : G → U(d_ρ)}, sends |g⟩ to Σ_ρ (d_ρ/|G|)^{1/2} Σ_{i,j} ρ(g)_{ij} |ρ, i, j⟩.

Question. Consider quantum algorithms for black-box group problems (including instances of the HSP, subgroup membership testing, order finding, normal closure, etc.) whose currently known correctness/efficiency proofs invoke only the abelian QFT (typically applied to abelian quotients or abelian subgroups of G). Does there exist any such algorithmic task for which replacing the abelian QFT step by a genuinely nonabelian QFT_G (together with appropriate measurement/post-processing) provably yields:
(a) a strictly more efficient quantum algorithm (asymptotically fewer queries to the black box, or smaller circuit complexity), or
(b) the solution of an HSP instance over a nonabelian group G for which no efficient algorithm based solely on abelian Fourier sampling is known?

Equivalently: characterize the additional algorithmic power, if any, that nonabelian quantum Fourier transforms provide over the abelian QFT in the black-box group model.
artifact.status_search_result: The nonabelian hidden subgroup problem remains open in general; while nonabelian Fourier sampling has yielded efficient algorithms for specific group families (e.g., certain metacyclic groups, Z_{p^r}⋊Z_p, Weyl–Heisenberg groups, extra-special p-groups), no general result establishes that nonabelian QFTs systematically outperform abelian QFTs in black-box group algorithms. Recent surveys (e.g., 2025 HSP survey) still list the comparative power of nonabelian Fourier sampling as an unresolved direction.

status_evidence.title: A survey about Hidden Subgroup Problem from a mathematical and cryptographic perspective
status_evidence.snippet: The nonabelian case... remains open; an efficient solution would give rise to an efficient quantum algorithm for graph isomorphism.
status_evidence.claim: The nonabelian HSP, and the comparative power of nonabelian Fourier sampling, remain open in general.

status_evidence.title: From optimal measurement to efficient quantum algorithms for the hidden subgroup problem over semidirect product groups
status_evidence.snippet: Efficient quantum algorithms have been found for a number of nonabelian hidden subgroup problems... certain metacyclic groups as well as all groups of the form Z_{p^r}⋊Z_p.
status_evidence.claim: Only partial advances have used nonabelian Fourier methods for specific group families.

status_evidence.title: The Hidden Subgroup Problem and Quantum Computation Using Group Representations
status_evidence.snippet: Fourier transforms over nonabelian groups are defined in terms of the irreducible complex representations of the group.
status_evidence.claim: Frames the use of nonabelian QFTs but does not settle their general algorithmic superiority.
